blockers: ESTIMAND MISMATCH (not fatal, but must be labelled). This is not a CRISPR screen hit list and the task was right to flag it. In BioGRID ORCS and in denali's Replogle arm the perturbed entity IS the entity called a hit (knock out gene G, G is a hit) - a causal/functional call. In Tahoe the perturbed entity is a small molecule and the hits are downstream transcripts - a response call. Both are gene-set-over-hit-list analyses and both inherit VIF = 1 + (m-1)*rho_bar, which src/audit_screen.py's own docstring asserts is screen-agnostic, so audit() genuinely applies. But the two distributions answer different questions and docs/CORPUS.md's own rule against conflating estimands applies with full force. Report as a separate stratum, never pooled into the ORCS corpus number.

PSEUDO-REPLICATION WOULD BE CATASTROPHIC IF POOLED - this is the real blocker. docs/CORPUS.md already documents that ONE publication contributing 340 of 1,272 screens (26.7%) distorted the median enough that the publication-level collapse moved the headline from 9.6% to 26.7%. Tahoe is 65,218 contrasts from ONE publication, ONE lab, ONE platform (Parse/Ultima), 14 plates. Pooled with ORCS's 1,272 it would be 98.1% of the combined corpus - a far worse version of the exact artifact that arm exists to expose. The design decision (separate stratum, hard cap, or publication-collapse to a single median) must be made BEFORE any number is computed, otherwise you generate a figure you then cannot quote.

TAHOE LANDS IN THE HIGHEST-CONFOUND STRATUM, so it will flatter denali. docs/CORPUS.md reports median R2 rising monotonically with hit-list size: 0.056 (20-100 hits) -> 0.184 (100-500) -> 0.226 (500-2,000) -> 0.263 (2,000+). VERIFIED from shard-0 row-group min(padj) statistics over 63 fully-contained contrasts: 0/63 had zero significant windows, and the median contrast has >=1 gene at padj<0.05 in 98.4% of its 1,000-gene windows - i.e. permissive, near-saturated hit lists. Tahoe will sit at the top of that gradient. Publishing a Tahoe median next to the ORCS median without the stratification is precisely the error the project exists to catch.

SECOND CONFOUND UNIQUE TO DE DATA THAT DENALI'S SIZE-ONLY MODEL WILL MIS-ATTRIBUTE. DESeq2 detection power scales with baseMean, so gene sets of highly-expressed genes (ribosome, OXPHOS) get more hits for a reason that is neither set size nor biology. Also rho_bar within a pathway is structurally far higher in co-expression data than in CRISPR screens - DE data is the motivating case for CAMERA (Wu & Smyth 2012, doi:10.1093/nar/gks461), already denali's own citation. Size-only R2 will absorb part of both and label it 'size'. UPSIDE: Tahoe's pseudobulk matrix is the one source that would let you actually compute rho_bar per set and use audit_screen.py's existing --corr / full-VIF path - but computing rho_bar IS a new analysis and is out of scope for a pure ingest.

DE METHOD IS INFERRED, NOT VERIFIED. The column set (baseMean, log2FoldChange, lfcSE, stat, pvalue, padj) is DESeq2's results() output verbatim, and the null pattern matches DESeq2 exactly (54.76% null lfc = baseMean 0; a further 21.8% null padj = independent filtering). But NO README I read documents the method. The Arc GitHub tahoe-100M README does not mention the pseudobulk DE table at all - it is an HF-side asset. UNVERIFIED: the DE method in prose, the FDR procedure, and the exact contrast specification beyond the HF obs_metadata note that 'DMSO_TF marks vehicle controls, use DMSO_TF along with plate to get plate matched controls'. Read the bioRxiv methods (Zhang et al. 2025, doi 10.1101/2025.02.20.639398) before publishing any number.

MY HIT-DENSITY SAMPLE IS ONE CELL LINE. Shard 0 is entirely A549, plate 1. The 63 contrasts I characterised are not representative of all ~50 cell lines, and the occupancy-inversion hit estimate saturates so it is a lower bound, not a count. The pass rate against denali's >=20-hit rule is verified at 100% for those 63 only; corpus-wide it is UNVERIFIED.

DRUG COUNT UNVERIFIED. Press material says ~1,200 drugs, but drug_metadata has only 379 rows and I did not count distinct drugs in the DE table (the HF /filter endpoint returns empty at this scale). sample_metadata = 1,344 rows, cell_line_metadata = 1,000 rows, gene_metadata = 62,710 rows - those are verified.

GENE NAMING IS MIXED. gene_name contains HGNC symbols (TSPAN6, DPM1), bare Ensembl IDs (ENSG00000274458, ENSG00000291316), and repeat/ncRNA labels (Metazoa_SRP-38). blockers: ANSWER TO THE ASKED QUESTION: Paperclip retrieves full text AND a supplementary layer, but that layer is a SCHEMA/PREVIEW, not the data. It cannot deliver supplementary table VALUES at scale. This bounds the atlas hard.

What the supplement layer actually contains: /papers/<id>/supplements/ lists real publisher filenames (mmc4.xlsx, 41467_2023_38594_MOESM4_ESM.xlsx, peerj-10-14369-s007.xlsx). Alongside each sits <file>.md.lines, which is a per-sheet SCHEMA SUMMARY only: sheet name, table name, exact row count, column names, dtypes, non-null counts, and exactly THREE sample values per column. No rows.

DECISIVE EVIDENCE: PMC10199906 is denali's own smarca4_ala audit (85 sets). Its 41467_2023_38594_MOESM4_ESM.xlsx.md.lines is 21 lines total. It names the exact columns the audit used ('# Genes in Gene Set (K)', '# Genes in Overlap (k)') and declares Rows: 85 -- but a grep for GOBP_/GOCC_/HALLMARK_ across that paper's entire content.lines returns only the two schema-summary lines. The 85 set names exist nowhere in the corpus. An audit denali already completed by hand is NOT reproducible from Paperclip.

Binary supplements are listed but unreadable. `paperclip cat` on the .xlsx returns: 'ERR: vsh: cat: Cannot read binary file' plus the hint 'Binary file. Download via GCS or use Python to process.' No GCS URI is exposed by `ls -l`, by meta.json, or anywhere in the CLI. There is no byte-level download path through the public CLI.

A partial value layer exists but is silently truncated and inconsistently present. Some papers additionally carry sections/'Supplement: <sheet>.lines' with real cell values. For PMC10573296 (htra3 audit) the 'Supplement: Analysis.lines' section holds genuine rows -- GeneRatio 38/198, BgRatio 221/18800, Count 38 -- but only 12 rows of the declared 1,985 (verified by counting distinct GO:/hsa IDs). The budget is byte-based and data-dependent: a sheet with long geneID strings gets ~12 rows; a narrow sheet got hundreds. Computing a floor off that preview would silently give R^2 on 12 of 1,985 sets. Mitigation exists: the declared 'Rows: N' line sits in the same document, so a parsed-rows == declared-rows guard is buildable and MUST be.

Coverage of even the schema layer is not universal. On denali's own 7 audited papers: PMC9703989 (yak-pasmc-s007) lists eight .xls/.xlsx supplements with NO .md.lines at all -- zero machine-readable layer. PMC10573296 (htra3) ships .zip supplements whose .zip.md.lines throws "'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xde in position 16" on read. So roughly 5 of 7 are usable even for triage.

Main-text tables ARE served with full values (verified: arx_2205.01285 renders a complete 'Gene Set Name | Genes in Set (K) | Genes in Overlap (k) | k/K | p-value | FDR q-value' table; arx_2107.05072 likewise with size 1618 / hits 16). But in-article enrichment tables are near-universally truncated to the top-10/20 sets by the authors. Fitting the floor on a p-value-ranked top-N subset is a different and biased statistic, not the screen's floor. Do not treat these as free screens.

Paperclip terms of service UNVERIFIED. paperclip.gxl.ai/terms, /terms-of-service and /legal all return HTTP 200 with the same SPA shell (no terms text); gxl.ai/terms returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch. I did not read a terms document from any primary source. This matters: the atlas plan is bulk automated querying of an authenticated commercial account (logged in as thealexschroeder@gmail.com) and then redistribution of statistics derived from what it returns. I cannot confirm either is permitted.

Redistribution of derived stats is mixed, not uniform. Under CC BY, redistributing a std.csv of (set, size, hits) plus an R^2 needs only attribution. Under CC BY-NC-ND it is not clean: NC bars commercial use and ND arguably bars redistributing a restructured copy of the table. PMC12354852 -- already committed as audits/external/gastric/std.csv -- is CC BY-NC-ND. That is an existing exposure in the repo, not a hypothetical, and is worth a licence column in the gallery.

sources.licence: No blanket licence exists; three different primary-source positions, all read verbatim this session. (1) NCBI/GEO — "NCBI itself places no restrictions on the use or distribution of the data contained therein. Nor do we accept data when the submitter has requested restrictions on reuse or redistribution. However, some submitters of the original data ... may claim patent, copyright, or other intellectual property rights ... NCBI cannot provide comment or unrestricted permission concerning the use, copying, or distribution of the information contained in the molecular databases." (2) EMBL-EBI Terms of Use, last revised 5 Feb 2024, plus the licensing policy page — "The Terms of Use also clarify that EMBL-EBI does not impose any additional restrictions on the use of data over those provided by the data owner"; CC0/CC-BY adoption is explicitly a forward-looking "next 5 years" roadmap, NOT the current state. (3) PMC (where the enrichment tables actually live) — "In the absence of a copyright statement, users should assume that standard copyright protection applies ... Users of PMC are directly and solely responsible for compliance with copyright." The ONLY definite, machine-readable, per-record licence in the whole chain is the PMC OA Web Service, which returns e.g. license="CC BY" for PMC8687118 (verified live).
sources.est_screens: For the question as asked — enrichment RESULT tables in GEO/ArrayExpress supplementary files — effectively ZERO. Measured: 0 of 199 supplementary filenames across 85 sampled GEO series (40 drawn from the 2,949 CRISPR-screen GSEs, 45 from the 3,896 GSEs whose own text mentions GSEA/"pathway analysis") matched any enrichment token; 0 of 78 ArrayExpress files across 25 studies (AE is ~80,759 studies, 430 CRISPR, and its file lists are dominated by .idf.txt/.sdrf.txt metadata). Enrichment output is essentially never deposited in a data repository — it is a paper artifact. The reservoir that does hold it is PMC/BioStudies S-EPMC: 145,589 PMC OA articles mention DAVID+enrichment, 57,737 mention clusterProfiler, 716 contain DAVID's literal output header "Functional Annotation Chart", and 6,065 OA articles combine "CRISPR screen" with enrichment/pathway analysis. But those are ARTICLE counts, not usable screens, and see the size-denominator blocker — my honest estimate of screens that would survive to a correct (size, hits) table is low hundreds at best, versus the 1,952 ORCS screens denali already has. Adjacent and genuinely useful: gene-level screen results DO appear in GEO at roughly 5% of files (11/199 measured: MAGeCK gene_summary, .rra/.sgrra, DESeq2 output), which denali could enrich itself.
sources.download_size: Discovery alone, not the payload: GEO exposes no bulk filename manifest, so enumerating names costs one HTTP directory listing per accession — 293,451 GSEs at NCBI's documented 10 req/s ceiling with an API key is ~8.5 hours of continuous polling for names only. The payload is unbounded and un-prefilterable: because no filename signals content, a harvest must download and sniff EVERY supplementary file, including the ~11% that are .zip bundles needing expansion. GEO series suppl payloads routinely run 10 MB-10 GB each (RAW.tar, bigwig, .hic seen in-sample), so a content-sniffing sweep of even the 2,949 CRISPR GSEs is multi-TB. Not feasible under any reasonable budget.
blockers: NO QUERYABLE HANDLE — the decisive finding. GEO's Entrez db=gds does expose a Supplementary Files field (SFIL), but it indexes ONLY file-type tokens, never filename words. Verified: txt[Supplementary Files]=1,369,750, csv=112,975, tar=35,412, xlsx=33,230, but GSEA=0, enrichment=0, DAVID=0, pathway=0, clusterProfiler=0 (each returning 'No items found', so the field exists and the term genuinely is not indexed). esummary confirms this independently — it returns suppfile:"CSV", a type, with no filenames at all. There is therefore no stable query for 'supplementary files that are enrichment tables'. Filenames are obtainable only one accession at a time via https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/series/GSE###nnn/GSE#####/suppl/ (works; modern series also carry filelist.txt).

THE ARTIFACT IS NOT THERE. Even with perfect enumeration there is nothing to find. 0 of 199 GEO supplementary filenames across 85 series, and 0 of 78 ArrayExpress files, resembled enrichment output. What GEO actually holds is counts matrices, bigwig, .hic, .bed, and raw tars. This is not a sampling artifact: the second sample was deliberately biased toward series whose own abstracts advertise GSEA/pathway analysis, and it still returned zero. Enrichment results are published as journal supplementary tables, not deposited as repository data.

NO NAMING CONVENTION IN THE ONE PLACE THEY DO EXIST. BioStudies mirrors PMC supplementary files as S-EPMC accessions with a clean JSON file-list API, but the names are publisher-assigned opaque IDs: 41 of 75 sampled names were pure boilerplate (mmc1.pdf, mmc2.csv, 1471-2105-10-275-S10.xls, 12859_2017_1674_MOESM1_ESM.xls, NIHMS466579-supplement-Supplementary.docx, btz831_supplementary_data.zip). Exactly 1 of 75 carried an enrichment token. So filename filtering cannot work there either, and BioStudies full-text search matches abstracts, not filenames (query 'DAVID_functional_annotation' returned 177,847 hits — tokenised OR, not a filename match).

FORMATS LIE. I downloaded S-EPMC8687118/mmc7.csv (CC BY, 7,299 bytes) and it is TAB-separated despite the .csv extension. Sampled extension mix across EPMC supplements: pdf 18, xls 17, xlsx 15, zip 8, tsv 6, docx 3, html 3, doc 2. A large fraction of the target population is locked inside PDF and DOCX, i.e. not machine-parseable at all, and 11% is zipped.

THE SIZE COLUMN MEANS THE WRONG THING — the scientific blocker, and the one that would sink the arm even if every engineering problem were solved. denali needs size = members MEASURED IN THIS SCREEN. Published enrichment tables report the annotation-database term size instead. Verified live against the g:Profiler API: a 6-gene query returns term_size=15 alongside effective_domain_size=5200, i.e. term_size is scoped to the annotated genome, not to the query's universe. g:Profiler's intersection_size is a usable hits, but its term_size is not a usable size unless the author passed a custom background restricted to the screened library — which most do not. Substituting the ontology size for the measured size changes the denominator of the no-biology floor, so the computed number would not be the quantity denali defines.

PUBLISHED TABLES ARE SELECTED ON THE OUTCOME. Enrichment supplements are conventionally truncated to significant terms (FDR<0.05). Regressing hits on size over a set list that was filtered by significance is selection on the dependent variable — the floor estimate would be biased by construction. INFERRED from publication practice, not measured in this session; I did not obtain enough parseable tables to quantify the truncation rate.

GSEA PROPER DOES NOT EMIT hits. The weighted-KS GSEA report carries SIZE, NES and FDR but no count of significant members, because it is not an over-representation test. So the single most commonly published enrichment format cannot fill denali's hits column at all. INFERRED from the method, not read from a primary source this session.

RATE LIMITS, read verbatim from NCBI's E-utilities guide (NBK25497): 'Without an API key, any site (IP address) posting more than 3 requests per second to the E-utilities will receive an error message'; with a key, 10/s; and NCBI asks that large jobs run on weekends or 21:00-05:00 US Eastern. Note the GEO FTP host is separate from eutils and its own policy was not verified — do not assume the 10/s figure covers directory-listing sweeps.

LICENCE IS INDIVIDUATED, NOT BLANKET. Both repositories explicitly decline to grant redistribution permission and push it to the submitter/copyright holder (exact wording in the licence field). For GEO there is no per-record licence field at all, so there is no programmatic way to filter to redistributable series. Only PMC OA articles carry a machine-readable per-article licence, and the PMC OA subset is a strict subset of PMC — the wider archive is standard-copyright by default.

CONCRETE ALTERNATIVE, worth more than this source. Do not chase enrichment tables; chase gene-level screen results and compute the enrichment yourself, which is what denali already does with BioGRID ORCS. 11 of 199 sampled GEO files (~5%) were gene-level result tables (GSE333678_mageck_gene_summary.csv.gz, GSE334916_results.gene_summary.txt.gz, GSE305962_*.rra.txt.gz, DESeq2 outputs), and the S-EPMC file I opened was itself a MAGeCK-style table with gene / p_value / significant columns. That path is strictly better on every axis: you control the universe so size is genuinely 'members measured', you get the full set list rather than a significance-truncated one, and the files are small. Its cost is that it is 'only_after_enrichment' — denali must run the ORA — and its marginal value over the 1,952 screens already in ORCS is modest, so scope it as an ORCS top-up, not a new atlas pillar.

sources.est_screens: 0 as-shipped. After a DE + program-scoring pipeline you would build: 1 screen from VCC-2025 (one H1 hESC CRISPRi experiment, 300 perturbations, 18,080 measured genes) and up to ~50 from Tahoe-100M (one per cancer cell line, ~1,138 drug-concentration perturbations each). scBaseCount yields 0 — it is observational, no perturbation, no hits. sources.download_size: VCC prefix totals 5,844.59 GB across 49 objects, but 5,810 GB of that is raw FASTQ. The only analysis-ready files are adata_Training.h5ad 15.482 GB + adata_Validation.h5ad 6.929 GB + adata_Test.h5ad 11.951 GB = 34.36 GB, plus three pert_counts CSVs (<10 KB each) and gene_names.csv (116,023 B, 18,080 genes). Tahoe-100M: 14 plate h5ad files = 337 GB, obs_metadata.parquet 2.29 GB, sample_metadata.parquet 65,636 B. scBaseCount 2026-01-12: not totalled, >502M cells across analysis/, h5ad/, metadata/, star_references/ — certainly multi-TB.
blockers: SHAPE MISMATCH — this is the disqualifying one. Arc ships single-cell count matrices (h5ad) and cell-count metadata. There is no DE table, no hit list, no gene-set table anywhere in the bucket. I did a full recursive listing of the virtual-cell-challenge/ prefix (49 objects) and read the Python tutorial notebook: the richest per-perturbation file is pert_counts_Training.csv with columns target_gene, n_cells, median_umi_per_cell. That is cells per perturbation, not members-measured / members-significant per set. Tahoe's sample_metadata.parquet is sample, plate, mean_gene_count, mean_tscp_count, mean_mread_count, mean_pcnt_mito, drug, drugname_drugconc — 1,344 rows, 380 distinct drugs, 1,138 distinct drug+concentration. Also no hits. Arc publishes pdex (MIT, 'parallel differential expression for single-cell perturbation sequencing') precisely because DE is something the consumer runs.

Neither of the two possible mappings to denali's shape works cleanly. Mapping A (ORCS-style, perturbation library as the measured universe): VCC's library is 300 genes. src/corpus_audit.py:96 requires len(measured) >= 10000 — this misses by 33x, and a 50-gene Hallmark set drawn from a 300-gene library will not clear the '>= 8 usable sets with >= 5 measured members' gate either. Tahoe has no gene library at all (drugs, not knockdowns). Mapping B (Replogle-style, transcriptome as the universe, perturbations as hits — which is what denali actually does, per DATA_DICTIONARY.md: n_present = Hallmark members measurable, n_hits_q05 = how many of 9,837 knockdowns moved the program): arithmetically valid, 18,080 genes clears the gate, but the entire VCC release collapses to ONE screen with a 300-perturbation hit axis instead of Replogle's 9,837.

Pseudo-replication, and denali already knows why this matters. If you split VCC into 300 per-perturbation 'screens' or Tahoe into ~57,000 drug-by-cell-line units to inflate the count, you reproduce the exact failure CORPUS.md identifies as its most fragile number — one publication contributing 340 of 1,272 screens, top five contributing 58.9%. Two publications contributing tens of thousands of units would swamp the atlas distribution outright.

Doing this requires a new enrichment analysis: download 34.4 GB (VCC) or 337 GB (Tahoe), run per-perturbation Wilcoxon vs NTC with BH FDR <= 0.05 (Arc's own stated method, per the 'Behind the Data' post), then score against gene sets. CLAUDE.md states ANALYSIS IS CLOSED — no new sweeps, no refits.

Requester Pays is a latent risk, not a current one. All three READMEs and the tutorial notebook warn that the new bucket 'is subject to Requester Pays' with 2 TB/month free. I could not confirm the flag: storage.buckets.get returns 401 anonymously. Empirically it is NOT being enforced today (see evidence) — but the flag can be flipped without notice, and if it is, an anonymous atlas build breaks.

The old public buckets are gone as documented. gs://arc-ctc-tahoe100 and gs://arc-scbasecount both return 401 on objects.list (access removed 2026-03-31). Any cached instructions pointing at them are dead.

virtualcellchallenge.org/datasets now 307-redirects to / — the 2025 dataset landing page no longer exists. The GCS bucket is the only live access path. Only 2025/ exists under virtual-cell-challenge/; the 2026 challenge (rules effective 2026-08-04, final test released 2026-10-22) has not deposited data into the atlas bucket yet.

Licence provenance is thinner than it looks, and I want this on the record. CC0 1.0 is asserted on Arc's own atlas web page, which is a primary source. But: there is no LICENSE file in the bucket root (LICENSE, LICENSE.txt, README.md, TERMS.md all 404), the GitHub repo ArcInstitute/arc-virtual-cell-atlas has license: None via the API, and the LaminDB mirror docs state only a citation request with no licence at all. The atlas page also pairs '© 2025' with the CC0 dedication, which is contradictory boilerplate (the CC0 waiver controls, but it is not immaculate drafting). A separate caveat applies to scBaseCount specifically: it is reprocessed SRA data, and Arc cannot CC0-dedicate third-party submissions it did not generate — irrelevant here since scBaseCount is unusable for denali anyway.
